title: Thermal Energy and Heat Transfer
seo_title: Year 9 Science: Thermal Energy Worksheets (Conduction, Convection, Radiation)
standard_text: Heating and thermal equilibrium: temperature difference between two objects leading to energy transfer from the hotter to the cooler one, through contact (conduction) or radiation; such transfers tending to reduce the temperature difference: use of insulators; energy changes on changes of state (qualitative); internal energy stored in materials.
meta_desc: Free Year 9 science worksheets on thermal energy: temperature and thermal energy, conduction, convection and radiation, cooling curves, conductors and insulators, and insulating homes. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Energy moves from hot to cold.
key_sub: Conduction in solids, convection in fluids, radiation through space.
body_html:
How to think about it

Energy is transferred from hotter places to cooler places.

  • Temperature (°C) measures how hot something is; thermal energy also depends on the amount of material.
  • Conduction through solids; convection in liquids and gases; radiation as infrared, even through a vacuum.
  • Insulators (air, foam, wool) slow heat transfer. Objects cool until they reach the temperature of their surroundings.
Example

Warm air rising from a heater?

A gas moves

Answer: convection

Example

Hot tea in a 20 °C room after hours?

Thermal equilibrium

Answer: 20 °C

Common mistakes

  • Thinking cold flows into things.
  • Mixing up temperature and thermal energy.
  • Thinking radiation needs particles.

faq.q: What is the difference between conduction, convection and radiation?
faq.a: Conduction passes energy through solids by vibrating particles. Convection carries energy as warm liquid or gas rises. Radiation transfers energy as infrared waves, even through a vacuum.

faq.q: Why do hot drinks cool quickly at first?
faq.a: The bigger the temperature difference from the surroundings, the faster energy is transferred, so cooling slows as the drink nears room temperature.
They are poor conductors, often because they trap air, so they slow down the transfer of energy.
